newsitem.title: USA: FDIC proposes less capital charge on service asset.
newsitem.headline: FDIC proposes less capital charge on service asset.

text.p: U.S. banks could hold substantially more mortgage servicing rights without a charge reducing their regulatory capital under a proposed rule released on Tuesday by federal bank regulators.
Under the proposal, the combined value of a bank's mortgage servicing rights and purchased credit card relationships could equal up to 100 percent of tier 1 capital without incurring a charge.
As banks have increasingly securitized and sold mortgage loans, a significant market has developed for mortgage servicing rights, the fees from administering the loans.

For many years, banks that sold loans but retained the lucrative servicing fees did not record the right to collect the stream of fees as an asset on their books. But banks that purchased identical servicing rights in the secondary market were required to record such rights as intangible assets.

Over the past two years, however, new accounting standards have required banks to record both types of servicing rights as intangible assets. And bank regulators generally deduct intangible assets, like goodwill, from a bank's tier 1 capital since those assets may be difficult to sell if the bank runs into trouble or is seized by the government.

But with a highly developed and liquid market for mortgage servicing rights, regulators decided that, up to a certain level, mortgage servicing rights should not be deducted from capital, according Robert Storch, chief of the accounting section in the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp's Division of Supervision.
The rights are "a liquid enough asset that we could include some reasonable amount in capital," Storch told reporters after an FDIC board meeting to discuss the proposal.
Purchased credit card relationships, the value of marketing other products to credit card holders, would still be subject to a separate limit of 25 percent of tier 1 capital.
Both types of assets would also be subject to a 10 percent "haircut," meaning the assets would be valued for regulatory purposes at the lower of book value or 90 percent of fair market value.
Comptroller of the Currency Eugene Ludwig backed the haircut as an appropriate and "prudent" treatment given the volatility in prices of servicing assets.
Servicing rights on credit cards and any other types of loans would continue to be treated as intangible assets, and fully deducted from capital, under the proposal.

Regulators asked for comments, due within 60 days, on whether servicing rights on other types of loans should receive special treatment. Regulators also asked for comments on the capital treatment of interest-only strips not in the form of securities.

As of the end of the of the first quarter, only one bank has run up against the old mortgage servicing asset limit of 50 percent, and a few more institutions hold between 25 and 50 percent, Storch said.
Regulators anticipate that many more banks will approach or exceed the 50 percent limit over the next few years as a result of the new accounting rules, he added.
